notes.meaning: The writer calls on his whole inner being to praise the Lord. God is revealed as truly great, dressed in royal honor and majesty throughout the physical world. Believers can rejoice that this great Ruler of all things is personally their God.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: In Eastern Orthodox worship, this psalm opens the evening service of Vespers as humanity's first act of praise to God as Creator.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars compare Psalm 104 to the ancient Egyptian Great Hymn to the Aten, while noting that the biblical poet directs all praise to the Lord rather than the sun.

notes.meaning: God is pictured as wrapping Himself in brilliant light as if putting on a royal robe. He unrolls the vast skies above the earth just like pitching a tent. Both the light and the heavens give continuous witness to His splendor.

The writer describes God building His upper rooms upon the waters high in the atmosphere. He rides upon the clouds as His royal chariot and travels swiftly on the wings of the wind. Even the fiercest skies remain entirely under His control.

God commands the rushing winds to carry His messages and uses flaming lightning as His swift servants. The natural elements promptly carry out whatever task He assigns them. The New Testament also points to this truth in Hebrews to show that heavenly angels are created servants of God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars argue that the original Hebrew poetically describes winds and lightning as God's natural messengers, whereas the ancient Greek translation read them as spiritual angels.

notes.meaning: God placed the earth firmly on its foundations so that it remains secure and balanced. It will not be shaken out of place until He finishes all His purposes for it. Believers can trust God's power to keep their world steady.

At the beginning of creation, deep water covered the earth like a heavy garment. The oceans rose so high that they buried even the highest mountains. This shows the state of the earth before God commanded the waters to divide.

At God's sharp command, the deep waters quickly pulled back. The sound of His thunder made the surging floods rush to where they belonged. Water has great destructive power, but it instantly obeys its Creator.

As the floodwaters drained away, mountains pushed upward and valleys sank down into place. Every hill and basin took the exact spot that God had appointed for it. He carefully shaped the land to provide a safe home for living creatures.

God set shoreline boundaries that the ocean cannot cross. He barred the rolling waves so they can never again drown the whole earth. Even simple sandy shores hold back the seas by God's sovereign decree.

Instead of letting waters flood the land, God sends freshwater springs down into the valleys. These streams wind quietly between the hills to bring moisture to the dry ground. God turns what could be a dangerous element into a blessing for the earth.

These mountain streams give fresh water to every wild animal of the field. Even wild donkeys roaming through the dry desert find their thirst satisfied. God's kindness reaches out to creatures that live far beyond human care.

Wild birds build their homes near these running streams and nest among the leafy branches. From their perches they sing out across the countryside. Their singing fills the quiet places of nature with praise to God.

God pours rain down from the clouds onto the hills that streams cannot reach. The land receives everything it needs from the fruit of His heavenly works. His showers cause even dry mountaintops to become fruitful.

God makes green grass grow to feed cattle and livestock. He also provides plants and grains for people to farm, bringing forth food from the dirt. God honors human farming while showing that He is the true giver of our daily food.

God provides wine to cheer the human heart and olive oil to make faces shine at celebrations. He also gives bread as a staple food to sustain life and renew physical strength. God is not stingy; He gives both what sustains life and what brings gladness.

The great trees of the forest drink their fill of rain and remain rich with sap. These include the massive cedars of Lebanon, which grew because God planted them rather than humans. God cares for the deepest woods just as carefully as an orchard.

Tall forest trees give many kinds of birds a safe shelter to build their nests. Storks make their homes high in the tops of the cypress trees. God gives each creature the exact instinct and refuge it needs.

High, rocky peaks provide a safe haven where wild mountain goats can climb. The rocky crags give small animals like the rock badger a place to hide from danger. Even steep and barren rocks have a valuable role in God's plan.

God made the moon to mark off the months and the seasons for Israel's calendar. The sun also follows an orderly path and knows the exact moment to set each day. These heavenly bodies are not gods to be worshipped, but servants designed to organize time.

When the sun goes down, God brings darkness so that nighttime can begin. In the dark, wild forest animals creep out from their dens to search for food. Night is part of God's wise schedule, giving wild creatures their time to roam.
Young lions roar through the darkness as they hunt for their prey. Their roaring is like a natural cry asking God to feed them. Even strong predators cannot survive unless God provides for them.

When the morning sun rises, the nighttime beasts retreat from the open land. They head back together and lie down to sleep in their dens. God's timing clears away dangerous beasts so people can move about safely.

With the wild animals resting, human beings head out to their daily labor. They work safely in the sunlight until evening brings an end to the day. God gives humanity both daytime for productive work and nighttime for rest.

The writer stops to wonder at the vast number of things God has made. Every creature was formed with marvelous wisdom, filling the whole earth with His treasures. Looking at creation should lead people to worship the wise God who designed it all.

The psalmist looks out at the great and wide Mediterranean Sea. Its waters teem with countless living things, both tiny creatures and massive animals. The ocean depths show God's power and skill just as clearly as the dry land.

Merchant ships travel across the open water to connect distant nations. In the same waters plays Leviathan, a huge sea animal that God formed to frolic in the waves. A sea creature that people feared is treated by God as a harmless pet.
All creatures on land and in the sea look to God with quiet dependence. They rely on Him to give them their food at the proper season. Every living thing is sustained day by day from God's hand.

When God scatters food across the earth, His creatures gather it up. When He opens His generous hand, every animal is satisfied with good nourishment. God's quiet care meets the daily needs of the whole living world.

If God hides His face by withholding His care, living things fall into panic. When He takes away their breath of life, they die and return to the soil. Life and death remain completely under God's control.

When God sends His life-giving Spirit or breath, fresh generations of creatures are born. In this way He preserves life and renews the face of the earth year after year. God never walks away from the world He made.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some Christian commentators link this verse to the future bodily resurrection of the dead and the final renewal of the created order.

notes.meaning: The writer prays that the Lord's glory will shine forever without fading. He asks that God will always take pleasure in His works, just as He did when creation was first completed. We should live in a way that gives our Maker reason to rejoice.

A single glance from God makes the whole earth tremble with fear. When He merely touches the mountains, smoke rises from them like Mount Sinai or an active volcano. His gentle touch carries terrifying power that creation cannot resist.

The psalmist makes a personal promise to sing praise to the Lord for as long as he lives. As long as he has breath, he will offer worship to his God. Remembering God's greatness as Creator should inspire a lifetime of thankful songs.

The writer desires that his private thoughts and songs will be pleasing to God. Thinking about God's mighty acts fills his own soul with deep gladness. True worship brings joy to the worshiper while honoring the Lord.

The psalm ends by asking God to remove wicked sinners so they no longer spoil His good world. The writer commands his soul once more to praise the Lord, closing with Hallelujah, which means praise the Lord. One day God will make His creation entirely clean from sin.
